name: Caffeine pre-workout

lead: Pre-workouts help you train with more energy, intensity and focus, which supports more muscle over time. Caffeine is the near-universal base, found in 86 percent of bestselling products in one analysis.

Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors, raising alertness and lowering perceived effort. It is described as a proven ergogenic aid at moderate doses, with documented improvements in sprint, endurance and strength outcomes. Other typical ingredients include creatine, beta-alanine, citrulline, amino acids and nitrates, where evidence is mixed and commercial doses are often below those studied. The effect on physique itself has not been directly studied.

paras: People mix a powder or drink a ready-to-drink product 20 to 45 minutes before training, usually on heavy days. Many use it only for key sessions or avoid it late in the day so it doesn't disrupt sleep.

High stimulant loads can raise blood pressure and cause anxiety and insomnia. Ingredient accuracy varies, and regulators have acted against stimulants sold in the category, such as ephedrine (2004) and DMAA (2012).

angle.text: Users take stimulant pre-workouts to get more energy and focus, train harder and build more muscle over time. Caffeine has the best support for improving performance; the effect on physique itself is not directly studied.

lead: Pre-workout supplements are multi-ingredient powders, capsules or drinks taken before training to increase energy, focus and endurance; caffeine is their near-universal base, found in 86% of bestselling products in one analysis.[1] Other typical ingredients include creatine, beta-alanine, citrulline, amino acids, nitrates and taurine.[1][2]

People use them to train harder or longer, on the view that more intense or more consistent sessions build more muscle and burn more fat over time. That chain, from a stimulant before a session to a better physique, is the appearance rationale; studies measure acute performance such as strength, endurance and power rather than appearance.[3][4] Pre-workout is a staple of gym culture and shows up in looksmaxxing discussion as a training aid for the muscle-and-leanness side of the project.

Caffeine itself is well studied as an ergogenic aid: the International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand reports small to moderate benefits for muscular endurance, strength, sprinting and jumping, with the most consistent benefits for aerobic endurance.[3] Evidence for the other blend ingredients is mixed, and doses in commercial products are often below those studied.[1][5][4] The category has a regulatory history: ephedrine was banned in supplements in 2004 and DMAA was acted against in 2012.[1][6][7] Wikipedia values the market at about 2.7 billion US dollars in 2008 and about 14.2 billion in 2022.[1]

paras: Pre-workout products are sold to people who lift weights, run or do other training, and are taken before a session. They come as powders mixed with water, capsules, tablets, liquids and bars, and many labels list a proprietary blend rather than individual amounts.[1] A profile of common ingredients found that caffeine, creatine and beta-alanine were among the most frequent, and Wikipedia reports a typical product contains about 18 ingredients.[1][2] Variants include sugar-free, creatine-free and stimulant-free versions for people who train in the evening or want to avoid caffeine.[1]

Each ingredient has its own claimed role. Caffeine is credited with alertness and a lower perception of effort; beta-alanine, found in 87% of leading formulas, with buffering fatigue in high-intensity efforts; creatine with performance and muscle growth; citrulline and arginine with a muscle 'pump' from blood flow; carbohydrates with sustained energy; and nitrates, usually from beetroot, taurine, tyrosine and B vitamins with assorted effects on endurance and focus.[1] Fat-loss-oriented versions add thermogenic stimulants such as synephrine and yohimbine.[1]

Dan Duchaine formulated Ultimate Orange in 1982 in Venice, California; it contained ephedra and was popular with bodybuilders.[1] Duchaine, a self-described steroid guru, is also known for the Underground Steroid Handbook (1981), and he died in January 2000.[8] Ephedra products drew complaints of high blood pressure, strokes, seizures, arrhythmia and heart attacks, and after the death of baseball pitcher Steve Bechler in February 2003 the FDA urged consumers to stop using ephedrine-alkaloid products. A final rule banning ephedrine-alkaloid supplements followed on 12 April 2004, and the Tenth Circuit upheld the ban in 2006.[1][6]

As ephedra left the market, creatine, widely used by athletes by the 1992 Olympics, became a popular alternative, and in the early 2000s manufacturers added arginine and citrulline for a muscle pump.[1] Chemist Patrick Arnold formulated a DMAA product in 2005, and Jack3d became prominent for its potency.[1] The FDA warned about DMAA products in April 2012, said in April 2013 that DMAA was not a legal dietary supplement, and won an appeal against Hi-Tech Pharmaceuticals in 2019; a US military sales ban dated from 2010.[1][7] Prohormones such as DHEA and CDMA, once common in pre-workouts, were formally banned in 2014.[1]

Top sellers in 2019 included Pre JYM, ENGN Shred and C4 Original.[1] Replacements for DMAA, such as DMBA and octodrine, have since appeared in some products.[1] The category has also spread outside gyms: a 2013 Hacker News post described developers using a pre-workout for focus and staying awake.[9]

Caffeine is a non-selective adenosine receptor antagonist, with A2A receptors central to its wakefulness effects; it also inhibits phosphodiesterase and affects dopamine signalling.[10] Onset is roughly 45 to 60 minutes and peak levels occur within 1 to 2 hours; it is metabolised mainly by the liver enzyme CYP1A2, and people differ in how quickly they clear it, for example smokers clear it faster and pregnancy slows it.[10] Regular users develop tolerance to some of its effects, such as the blood-pressure and alertness response, and may experience mild withdrawal such as headache or fatigue after stopping.[10]

Beta-alanine is converted in muscle to carnosine, which buffers the acid produced during high-intensity exercise and is proposed to delay fatigue; Wikipedia reports links to improved performance in efforts of roughly half a minute to ten minutes, and a harmless dose-dependent tingling sensation. The International Society of Sports Nutrition published a position stand on it in 2015.[11] Citrulline is a by-product of nitric oxide production from arginine and is promoted for athletic performance; Wikipedia's general citrulline article says it remains under preliminary research.[12] A trial of citrulline malate in untrained young men found it did not improve muscle recovery after resistance exercise.[13]

Wikipedia describes moderate caffeine intake as improving sprinting, time trials, endurance, power and muscular strength, and lowering perceived exertion, and calls it a proven ergogenic aid.[10] The ISSN position stand summarises acute benefits as small to moderate and reports that effects vary between individuals; it notes that very high intakes bring a high incidence of side effects without being required for an ergogenic effect.[3]

A brief review of multi-ingredient pre-workout supplements found a substantial body of evidence that acute consumption may improve muscular endurance and subjective mood, with mixed results for force and power outcomes; direct comparisons are hard because of undisclosed proprietary blends.[4] Reviews cited by Grokipedia attribute benefits mainly to well-dosed caffeine and beta-alanine rather than blend synergy.[5]

Users often report feeling more energised, though Wikipedia notes there is little quantitative proof of the subjective effect.[1] The appearance payoff, more muscle and less fat, depends on what the extra training effort adds up to over months; the available trials measure performance in single sessions or a few weeks.[14][15][16]

Common effects of caffeine include anxiety, jitteriness and insomnia, with anxiety more likely above roughly 300 to 400 mg.[10] Energy-drink-level intakes of about 320 mg have been linked to short-term blood-pressure and palpitation effects.[10] Health Canada advises a maximum of 400 mg per day for healthy adults, and the European Food Safety Authority likewise reports no safety concern up to 400 mg per day for non-pregnant adults, with 200 mg per day acceptable in pregnancy.[10] Pre-workouts can also contain stimulants such as synephrine and higenamine linked to cardiovascular risk, and ingredient accuracy and contamination have been reported as problems; one study found melamine in up to half of analysed blends.[1] The FDA does little pre-market control, and the company is responsible for safety.[1]

A 2025 integrative review of 24 studies found pre-workout supplements associated with improved performance and with possible cardiovascular changes classed as adverse or cardioprotective, and concluded that the literature is limited and conflicting.[17] A review of food-supplement categories reported contamination with unauthorised substances in pre-workout, fat-burner and similar products, and that some ingredients are prohibited in sport.[18] A case report has described pancreatitis associated with pre-workout use.[19] A meta-analysis of 24 studies found caffeine reduced total sleep time by about 45 minutes and sleep efficiency by 7%, and estimated that a standard pre-workout serving (217.5 mg caffeine) should be consumed roughly 13 hours before bedtime to avoid shortened sleep.[20]

DMAA has been associated with at least five deaths according to Wikipedia, including runner Claire Squires in the 2012 London Marathon, where a coroner called it 'probably an important factor'; a 2013 US Department of Defense review panel found the evidence did not conclusively establish causation but recommended keeping the sales ban.[7] Beta-alanine causes a harmless tingling sensation, and DMAA replacements such as DMBA and octodrine have reportedly caused similar effects.[1][11]

sections.h: Variants and how people use them
paras: Users choose among stimulant formulas, stimulant-free formulas for evening training, 'pump' formulas heavy on citrulline and nitrates, and 'shred' formulas that add thermogenics for people cutting fat.[1] Some people skip commercial blends and take caffeine on its own, in coffee, tablets or powder, and a bench-press crossover study compared a multi-ingredient pre-workout with the same caffeine alone.[14] Product labels commonly advise a limit on servings per day and advise consulting a healthcare professional, and the FDA gives the same advice.[1]

A bench-press crossover study compared a multi-ingredient pre-workout (beta-alanine, citrulline malate, arginine alpha-ketoglutarate, taurine, tyrosine, caffeine) with an equivalent dose of anhydrous caffeine alone on strength and psychological measures.[14] A 2025 double-blind randomised trial in middle-aged adults compared pre-workout multi-ingredient supplements with carbohydrate alone and found similar resistance-training outcomes.[15] A randomised double-blind crossover study examined a multi-ingredient supplement on anaerobic performance,[21] and a 28-day study of the product NO-Shotgun combined with resistance training measured body composition, strength, muscle mass and safety markers in men.[16] A trial of citrulline malate in untrained young men found it did not improve muscle recovery after resistance exercise.[13]

Registered trials have studied caffeinated versus non-caffeinated pre-workout on resistance exercise performance (24 participants),[22] multi-ingredient pre-workout and energy expenditure during running,[23] and caffeine-based supplement effects on muscle power.[24] These registered studies are small (12 to 36 participants) and measure performance rather than changes in physical appearance.

Pre-workout is sold as a dietary supplement; the FDA does not pre-approve supplements and monitors adverse-event reports after sale, according to Wikipedia.[1] Ingredient lists often use proprietary blends, and some companies use third-party testing to address label accuracy.[1][2] Sports bodies including WADA prohibit DMAA, and athletes have been sanctioned after positive tests.[7]

lore.intro: Pre-workout is a staple of gym culture and appears in looksmaxxing discussions as a training aid rather than an appearance product.[9]

claims.claim: A pre-workout makes training sessions harder and more productive.
The ingredients in a blend work better together than caffeine alone.
Citrulline gives a better pump and faster recovery.
Beta-alanine delays fatigue in hard sets.
A pre-workout late in the day does not affect sleep.
Products contain what the label says.
